Representatives elections in Texas''' were held on November 8, 2022, to elect the 38 [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representatives]] from [[Texas]], one from each of the state's 38 [[Texas's congressional districts|congressional districts]]. The state gained two seats after the results of the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]]. The elections coincided with [[2022 United States House of Representatives elections|other elections]] to the House of Representatives, [[2022 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the [[United States Senate]], and various [[2022 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2022 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Primary elections took place on March 1, with primary runoffs scheduled for May 24 for districts where no candidate received over 50% of the vote. [[Republican Party of Texas|Republicans]] had gained one seat in the House due to a [[2022 Texas's 34th congressional district special election|special election]] in the [[Texas's 34th congressional district|34th district]] seeing [[Mayra Flores]] succeed [[Filemon Vela Jr.|Filemon Vela]] and become the first Mexican-born congresswoman.{{Cite web|last=Martinez|first=Marissa|title=Republican Mayra Flores flips Dem House seat in South Texas|url=https://www.politico.com/news/2022/06/14/republican-mayra-flores-flips-dem-house-seat-in-south-texas-00039717|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=POLITICO|date=June 14, 2022|language=en}}{{Cite news|last=Medina|first=Jennifer|date=June 15, 2022|title=Republicans flip a Democratic-held House seat in South Texas, at least for now.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/06/14/us/politics/mayra-flores-texas-election.html|access-date=February 8, 2023|issn=0362-4331}} During the 2022 elections, the [[Texas Democratic Party|Democrats]] and Republicans each gained one of the two seats Texas gained through reapportionment.{{Cite web|last=Bludau|first=Janelle|date=November 8, 2022|title=Republican Wesley Hunt claims victory in Texas' newly created 38th Congressional District|url=https://www.khou.com/article/news/politics/republican-wesley-hunt-wins-texas-congressional-district-38/285-44d63ad6-95ec-4b18-b9ae-172e41429ae9|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=khou.com|language=en-US}}{{Cite web|date=November 8, 2022|title=Texas election: Lloyd Doggett wins newly-created U.S. House District 37|url=https://www.kxan.com/news/your-local-election-hq/texas-election-voters-decide-newly-created-u-s-house-district-37-representative/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=KXAN Austin|language=en-US}} While Republicans flipped the [[Texas's 15th congressional district|15th district]], Democrats flipped back the 34th district, and retained the [[Texas's 28th congressional district|28th district]], dashing Republican hopes of a [[Wave elections in the United States|red wave]] in the [[Lower Rio Grande Valley|Rio Grande Valley]].{{Cite news|last=Alvey|first=Rebekah|date=November 9, 2022|title=Dashing GOP hopes of South Texas red wave, Dems Gonzalez and Cuellar survive 2022 midterms|work=[[The Dallas Morning News]]|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/news/elections/2022/11/08/texas-midterm-elections-2022-the-new-us-house-of-representatives-delegation/|access-date=February 8, 2023}} This resulted in a net gain of one seat for both parties. {{Horizontal TOC|nonum=yes|limit=2}} ==Redistricting== {{Main|Redistricting in Texas}} [[File:Texas Congressional Districts, 118th Congress (new version).svg|400px|thumb]] The [[Texas Legislature]] drew new maps for Texas' congressional districts to account for the two new congressional districts it gained through the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]]. The [[Republican Party of Texas|Republican Party]] had a trifecta in the Texas Government at the time, giving them full control of the redistricting process.{{Cite web|last=Ura|first=Alexa|date=April 26, 2021|title=Texas will gain two seats in Congress as residents of color drive population gains|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/04/26/texas-congress-seats-gain/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}} Legislators drew the maps for the state during a special session in Fall 2021.{{Cite web|last=Kao|first=Alexa Ura and Jason|date=September 20, 2021|title=Texas Republicans have the redistricting tools to preserve their power. Here's how they can do it.|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/09/20/texas-redistricting-special-session/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}} The maps that passed were widely criticized as racial and partisan gerrymanders designed to keep Republicans in power and reduce the voting power of minorities.{{Cite web|last1=Li|first1=Michael|last2=Boland|first2=Julia|date=December 7, 2021|title=Anatomy of the Texas Gerrymander|url=https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/anatomy-texas-gerrymander|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=www.brennancenter.org|publisher=[[Brennan Center for Justice]]|language=en}}{{Cite news|last=Rodriguez|first=Jessica|date=July 25, 2022|title=SMU team generated 1.5M district maps, but none were as gerrymandered as Texas' pick|work=[[The Dallas Morning News]]|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/news/2022/07/25/smu-team-generated-15m-district-maps-but-none-were-as-gerrymandered-as-texas-pick/|access-date=February 8, 2023}} News sources specifically noted that both of Texas' new congressional districts were majority white, despite voters of color making up 95% of the state's growth in the previous decade.{{Cite web|last=Ura|first=Alexa|date=October 19, 2021|title=Texas Republicans send Gov. Greg Abbott a new congressional map that protects GOP power, reduces influence of voters of color|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/10/18/texas-congressional-maps-redistricting/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Limón|first=Elvia|date=October 25, 2021|title=Gov. Greg Abbott signs off on Texas' new political maps, which protect GOP majorities while diluting voices of voters of color|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/10/25/2021-texas-redistricting-explained/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}}{{Cite web|last=Rakich|first=Nathaniel|date=February 28, 2022|title=Texas May Have The Worst Gerrymander In The Country|url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/videos/texas-may-have-the-worst-gerrymander-in-the-country/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220228152529/https://fivethirtyeight.com/videos/texas-may-have-the-worst-gerrymander-in-the-country/|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 28, 2022|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=FiveThirtyEight|language=en-US}}{{Cite news|last=Dallas Morning News Editorial Board|date=October 12, 2021|title=Texas redistricting needs to go back to the drawing board|work=[[The Dallas Morning News]]|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/opinion/editorials/2021/10/12/texas-redistricting-needs-to-go-back-to-the-drawing-board/|access-date=February 8, 2023}} Unlike before the [[2012 United States House of Representatives elections in Texas|2012 elections]], Texas' maps did not have to pass preclearance under Section 5 of the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]], as the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] had ruled preclearance unconstitutional through ''[[Shelby County v. Holder]]'' in 2013.{{Cite web|last=Ura|first=Alexa|date=September 17, 2021|title=In a changing Texas, Republicans will begin redistricting with more freedom to draw their maps|url=https://www.texastribune.org/2021/09/17/texas-redistricting-preclearance/|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=The Texas Tribune|language=en}}{{Cite news|last=Liptak|first=Adam|date=June 25, 2013|title=Supreme Court Invalidates Key Part of Voting Rights Act|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/06/26/us/supreme-court-ruling.html|access-date=February 8, 2023|issn=0362-4331}} Despite this, the [[United States Department of Justice|Justice Department]] sued the state of Texas after the map's passage, arguing that they violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.{{Cite web|date=December 6, 2021|title=Justice Department Files Lawsuit Against the State of Texas to Challenge Statewide Redistricting Plans|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-files-lawsuit-against-state-texas-challenge-statewide-redistricting-plans|access-date=February 8, 2023|website=www.justice.gov|language=en}} On October 26, 2021, Gonzalez announced that he would run for election in the neighboring [[Texas's 34th congressional district|34th district]], while still serving District 15 until 2023. The district was also significant as, despite its historical Democratic lean, [[Donald Trump]] came within two points of winning it in [[2020 United States presidential election in Texas|2020]], and the newly drawn 15th is even more Republican than its predecessor.
